_note: Plain-language financial guidance for the Learn tab. Static, educational, not advice.

articles.title: How your credit score actually moves
body: Your score is a summary of how you handle borrowed money. The biggest factors are paying on time and how much of your available credit you're using (your "utilization").
Small month-to-month swings of a few points are normal. Large drops usually have a specific cause: a missed payment, a new account, a big balance jump, or a hard inquiry.
When Mosaic flags a change, it's showing you the cause — not deciding whether it's bad. You decide.

articles.title: Hard vs. soft inquiries
body: A soft inquiry (checking your own report, a pre-approval offer) does not affect your score and isn't visible to lenders.
A hard inquiry happens when you apply for credit — a card, loan, or mortgage. It can shave a few points and stays on your report about two years.
The warning sign is a hard inquiry from a company you never applied to. That can mean someone is trying to open credit in your name.

articles.title: Spotting identity theft on your report
body: Red flags: an account you don't recognize, a hard inquiry you didn't authorize, a collection for a debt that isn't yours, or an address you've never lived at.
One unfamiliar item can be an error. Several appearing in a short window — especially a new account plus new inquiries — is the classic identity-theft pattern.
If you see this, don't panic and don't pay anything yet. Place a fraud alert, then dispute the items in writing (Mosaic drafts the letter for you).

articles.title: Fraud alert vs. credit freeze
body: A fraud alert is free, lasts one year, and tells lenders to verify your identity before opening credit. You place it with one bureau and it notifies the other two.
A credit freeze is stronger: it blocks new credit from being opened at all until you lift it. It's also free, but you must place and lift it with each bureau separately.
Use an alert for "something looks off, be cautious." Use a freeze when you're confident fraud has occurred or want maximum protection.

articles.title: Your right to dispute and validate
body: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, you can dispute anything inaccurate on your report, and the bureau must investigate — usually within 30 days.
For a collection you don't recognize, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act lets you demand validation before paying. Make the collector prove the debt is yours and the amount is right.
Always keep it in writing and keep copies. Mosaic generates the letter; you review, edit, and send it yourself — nothing is filed automatically.
